citations.quote:
Fix a finite number $K\ge1$ of causes on a probability space. Let
$T_1,\ldots,T_K$ be measurable event times with values in $[0,\infty)$, and
assume that the minimum is attained by a unique cause almost surely. The
**observed first failure time** and its **cause** are
$$T:=\min_{1\le j\le K}T_j,\qquad D:=\min\{j:T_j=T\}\in\{1,\ldots,K\},$$
so $D$ is the smallest label attaining the minimum. For each $k$,
$$\{D=k\}=\bigcap_{j<k}\{T_k<T_j\}\cap\bigcap_{j>k}\{T_k\le T_j\},$$
which is measurable; the assumed almost-sure uniqueness makes the tie-break
irrelevant except on a null set.
No independence among the latent times $T_j$ is assumed. When an external
right-censoring time $C$ is present, the observation is
$(U,\delta,D^{\mathrm{obs}})$, where $U=\min(T,C)$ and
$\delta=\mathbf 1\{T\le C\}$ as in
[[def-event-time-observation-schemes]], and $D^{\mathrm{obs}}=D$ when
$\delta=1$; the cause label is absent when $\delta=0$. Thus an event tied with
censoring is recorded as an event.

The **all-cause survival function** is $S(t):=\mathbb P(T>t)$ for $t\ge0$.
For $u>0$, write $S(u-):=\mathbb P(T\ge u)$; this is the left limit of $S$
by continuity from above for measures
([[thm-continuity-from-above-for-measures]]). Set $S(0-):=1$.

For each cause $k$, its **event subdistribution measure** and
**cause-specific cumulative-incidence function** are
$$\nu_k(B):=\mathbb P(T\in B,D=k),\qquad F_k(t):=\nu_k([0,t])=\mathbb P(T\le t,D=k).$$
for Borel $B\subseteq[0,\infty)$ and $t\ge0$. The **cause-specific hazard
measure** is the measure with density
$$w(u):=\begin{cases}1/S(u-),&S(u-)>0,\\0,&S(u-)=0\end{cases}$$
relative to $\nu_k$:
$$\Lambda_k(B):=\int_B w(u)\,\nu_k(du),\qquad d\Lambda_k(u)=w(u)\,\nu_k(du).$$
The extension of $u\mapsto S(u-)$ by the constant $1$ for $u<0$ is
nonincreasing on $\mathbb R$ and therefore Borel measurable
([[thm-monotone-real-functions-are-borel-measurable]]), so $w$ is a
nonnegative Borel function and this measure is defined by
[[def-measure-with-density]]. It may have infinite total mass; no finite-horizon
integrability is assumed in this definition.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. The **measure with density $f$ relative
to $\mu$** is the measure
$$f\,d\mu:\mathcal A\to[0,+\infty],\qquad (f\,d\mu)(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu,$$
whose measure property is supplied by
[[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]].

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int g\,d(f\,d\mu)=\int gf\,d\mu.$$

Every monotone function $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ in the sense of
[[def-monotone-function]] is Borel measurable.

derivations.claim: The set function $\nu_k(B)=\mathbb P(T\in B,D=k)$ is a finite measure: it is the restriction of the law of $(T,D)$ to the measurable cause slice $D=k$, so disjoint Borel sets have disjoint preimages and probability countable additivity applies.
The function $s(u):=S(u-)=\mathbb P(T\ge u)$ is nonincreasing, hence Borel by [F4]. Thus $R:=\{u:s(u)>0\}$ is Borel and $w=s^{-1}\mathbf 1_R$ is nonnegative Borel.

The set $R^c$ is an upper interval. If $R^c=[a,\infty)$, then $\nu_k(R^c)\le\mathbb P(T\ge a)=s(a)=0$. If $R^c=(a,\infty)$, then $\{T>a\}=\bigcup_{m\ge1}\{T\ge a+1/m\}$ and each event on the right has probability $s(a+1/m)=0$; hence again $\nu_k(R^c)=0$. The empty case is immediate.

Applying [F3] with $g(u)=\mathbf 1_{[0,t]}(u)s(u)$ gives $\int_{[0,t]}s(u)\,d\Lambda_k(u)=\int_{[0,t]}s(u)w(u)\,d
u_k(u)=\int_{[0,t]}\mathbf 1_R(u)\,d
u_k(u)=
u_k([0,t])=F_k(t)$. The penultimate equality uses step 3.1, so this proves the measure-valued identity, including atoms and $t=0$.

Suppose $
u_k(du)=f_k(u)\,du$ and $S(u)>0$ for every $u\in(0,t]$. For each integer $m\ge1$, the set $A_m:=\{u\in(0,t]:\mathbb P(T=u)\ge1/m\}$ has at most $m$ points, since distinct singleton events are disjoint and their probabilities sum to at most $1$. Every positive atom belongs to some $A_m$, so $A:= igcup_{m\ge1}A_m$ is countable and therefore Lebesgue-null. For $0<u\le t$, the definitions $s(u)=\mathbb P(T\ge u)$ and $S(u)=\mathbb P(T>u)$ give $s(u)-S(u)=\mathbb P(T=u)$; hence $s(u)=S(u)$ outside $A$. Also $s(u)\ge S(u)>0$, so $w(u)=1/s(u)$ on $(0,t]$. Since $d
u_k=f_k\,du$, [F1, F3] give $d\Lambda_k=w f_k\,du$, whose density agrees with $f_k/S=\lambda_k$ Lebesgue-a.e. on $(0,t]$. Finally, $
u_k(\{0\})=0$ because $
u_k$ has a Lebesgue density, so the point $0$ contributes nothing to either side of step 4.1; substituting the density on $(0,t]$ into that identity gives the stated formula, including $t=0$.

risk_review.notes: Independently checked every proof step and all four direct suppliers. nu_k is a finite cause-slice measure; s=P(T>=u) is Borel. Its zero set is an upper interval; in the closed-endpoint case P(T>=a)=0, and in the open-endpoint case the countable union of {T>=a+1/m} has probability zero. s(0)=1 excludes the whole-domain zero-set case. Density integration yields s*w=1_R nu_k-a.e., hence the identity for every k and finite t including t=0, atoms and exhausted survival. For the density specialization only nu_k needs a Lebesgue density; all-cause atoms form a countable null set, so s=S almost everywhere even if other causes have atoms. Stated S>0 on (0,t] permits f_k/S there; density excludes the baseline atom. Zero cause measure, K=1, empty integrals, terminal atoms and possibly infinite hazard mass checked; no sigma-finiteness of hazard or AC is assumed. Tartu slides16-17 supply continuous context; local density supplier proves the stronger measure identity. Reader/refuter evidence reviewed; no defect.

**Input:** A finite sample of $n\ge1$ right-censored records
$(U_i,\delta_i,D_i^{\mathrm{obs}})$ for $K$ causes, using
$U_i=\min(T_i,C_i)$ and $\delta_i=\mathbf 1\{T_i\le C_i\}$ from
[[def-event-time-observation-schemes]]. The observed cause label
$D_i^{\mathrm{obs}}\in\{1,\ldots,K\}$ is present only when $\delta_i=1$.
Fix a horizon $t\ge0$.

The pointwise population target is
$\psi_t:=(S(t),F_1(t),\ldots,F_K(t))\in\mathbb R^{K+1}$; the algorithm
returns its finite-sample estimate.

For each event time $u\in[0,t]$, define the risk count and cause-specific event
counts by
$$Y(u):=\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf 1\{U_i\ge u\},\qquad \Delta N_k(u):=\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf 1\{U_i=u,\delta_i=1,D_i^{\mathrm{obs}}=k\},\qquad \Delta N(u):=\sum_{k=1}^K\Delta N_k(u).$$
All subjects with an event at $u$ are included in $Y(u)$, so tied observed
failures are grouped before updating and $Y(u)\ge\Delta N(u)>0$ at every
event time. Censorings at $u$ do not contribute to $\Delta N(u)$; a subject
with $T_i=C_i=u$ is an event by the stated $T_i\le C_i$ convention.

**Procedure:**

1. List the distinct observed event times $u\le t$ in increasing order, with
   all causes at a common time grouped into the same counts $\Delta N_k(u)$.
2. Initialize $\widehat S(0-)=1$ and $\widehat F_k(0-)=0$ for each cause.
3. At each listed $u$, set
   $$\widehat F_k(u)=\widehat F_k(u-)+\widehat S(u-)\frac{\Delta N_k(u)}{Y(u)},\qquad \widehat S(u)=\widehat S(u-)\left(1-\frac{\Delta N(u)}{Y(u)}\right).$$
4. Keep the estimates constant between event times and return
   $(\widehat S(t),\widehat F_1(t),\ldots,\widehat F_K(t))$.

Equivalently,
$$\widehat S(t)=\prod_{0\le u\le t:\,\Delta N(u)>0}\left(1-\frac{\Delta N(u)}{Y(u)}\right),\qquad \widehat F_k(t)=\sum_{0\le u\le t:\,\Delta N(u)>0}\widehat S(u-)\frac{\Delta N_k(u)}{Y(u)}.$$
The convention at $u=0$ allows a baseline event; when there is none, these
formulas agree with the $(0,t]$ product-limit convention in
[[def-nelson-aalen-kaplan-meier-greenwood-estimators]].

This procedure is a finite-sample definition, not a consistency or variance
theorem. A common sampling setup for interpreting it as an estimator of a
population law has IID subject records ([[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]),
independent censoring $C\perp(T,D)$ ([[def-independent-random-elements]]), and
$\mathbb P(C\ge t)>0$, a positive censoring-support condition through $t$.
These are model assumptions, not consequences of the formula.
This item does not invoke a counting-process compensator, martingale bracket,
or process-limit result.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be an experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). A **statistic** with target
measurable space $(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$ is a measurable map
$T:(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)\to(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$, where measurability
means that $T^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal A$ for every $B\in\mathcal B$
([[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]). If
$\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal Y$ is an estimand ([[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]])
and its target set $\mathcal Y$ is equipped with $\mathcal B$, a statistic
$\widehat\psi$ with this same target space is an **estimator of $\psi$**.
The value $\widehat\psi(x)$ is the estimate at observed data $x$. Giving
$\mathcal Y$ a measurable structure is an additional choice; this definition
does not assert that $\psi$ is measurable as a function of the parameter.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ and $(Y,\mathcal{B})$ be measurable spaces
([[def-measurable-space]]). A function $f : X \to Y$ is **measurable** when

$$f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \qquad \text{for every } B \in \mathcal{B}.$$

Equivalently, the family

$$\mathcal{C}_f := \{\, B \subseteq Y : f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \,\}$$

is a sigma-algebra on $Y$ containing $\mathcal{B}$.

derivations.claim: For every $i,j$, the predicates $U_i\le t$, $U_i\le U_j$, $U_i=U_j$, and each finite-valued cause-status predicate define Borel subsets of $\mathcal X$: the coordinate-comparison sets are closed in the Euclidean sample space, and status slices are Borel in the finite status space. Hence $Y(U_i)$ and $\Delta N_k(U_i)$ are finite sums of measurable indicators by [F1] and [F4]. If $i$ is an event at $u=U_i$, then its indicator is included in $Y(u)$ and in $\Delta N(u)$, so $Y(u)\ge\Delta N(u)\ge1$.

For each event record the ratio $\Delta N_k(U_i)/Y(U_i)$ has finite range, since both counts lie in $\{0,\ldots,n\}$ and the denominator is in $\{1,\ldots,n\}$; each level set is a finite union of Borel count-level sets, so the ratio is measurable. The indicator selecting the first record at each distinct event time and the ordering of the at most $n$ event times are also determined by finitely many Borel equalities and inequalities. The updates in [F1] therefore form finite sums and products of measurable functions; [F4] makes every coordinate of the output vector measurable. By [F2] and [F3], this vector is a statistic in the experiment fixed in the Statement, and step 1.1 proves its denominators are positive.

Steps 1.1 and 2.1 use U_i<=t and U_i>=u, so events at t and baseline u=0 are included.

For an experiment on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, let
$\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ denote the set of all probability measures
on that measurable space. Its **parametric statistical model** is the parameter
map
$$
\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\qquad \mathsf P(\theta)=P_\theta,
$$
regarded together with its parameter set and sample space
([[def-statistical-experiment]]). The map need not be injective. Unless a
measurable structure on $\Theta$ is supplied separately, no measurability of
$\mathsf P$ is asserted.

In a parametric model $\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$,
two parameter values $\theta,\eta\in\Theta$ are **observationally
equivalent**, written $\theta\sim\eta$, if and only if
$$
P_\theta=P_\eta,
$$
that is, $P_\theta(A)=P_\eta(A)$ for every $A\in\mathcal A$
([[def-parametric-statistical-model]]). Equivalent parameter values therefore
give exactly the same sampling law. No distinctness of $\theta$ and $\eta$ is
required.

For a parametric model with parameter set $\Theta$, an **estimand** or
**parameter target** is a specified function
$$
\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal T_0,
$$
where $\mathcal T_0$ is a set of target values
([[def-parametric-statistical-model]]). This definition imposes no measurable
structure on $\Theta$ or $\mathcal T_0$ and does not require $\psi$ to determine
the full parameter value.

An estimand $\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal T_0$ is **identifiable** in a parametric
model $\mathsf P$ when
$$
P_\theta=P_\eta\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\psi(\theta)=\psi(\eta)\qquad(\theta,\eta\in\Theta),
$$
or equivalently when $\psi$ is constant on each set of parameter values with
the same sampling law ([[def-parametric-statistical-model]],
[[def-observational-equivalence]], [[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]]).
The model is **identifiable** when its identity target
$\operatorname{id}_\Theta:\Theta\to\Theta$ is identifiable, equivalently
when $\mathsf P$ is injective.

derivations.claim: Let $\psi(\theta)$ be the full joint law of $(T_1,T_2)$ under parameter $\theta$. This is an estimand by [F4]. The two laws specified above differ: under $\theta=0$, $\mathbb P(T_2=2)=1/2$, while under $\theta=1$, $\mathbb P(T_2=2)=0$.

Under either parameter, the first event is at time $1$. The outcome $(T,D)=(1,1)$ has probability $1/2$ from the atom with $T_1=1$, and $(T,D)=(1,2)$ has probability $1/2$ from the atom with $T_2=1$; no other observed pair occurs. Thus the two pushforward sampling laws are equal, so the parameters are observationally equivalent by [F2]–[F3].

Step 1.1 gives $\psi(0)\ne\psi(1)$, while step 1.2 gives equal sampling laws. This violates the defining implication in [F5], so the latent joint law is not identifiable from the observed first time and cause.

$$\widehat S(t)=\prod_{0\le u\le t:\,\Delta N(u)>0}\left(1-\frac{\Delta N(u)}{Y(u)}\right),\qquad \widehat F_k(t)=\sum_{0\le u\le t:\,\Delta N(u)>0}\widehat S(u-)\frac{\Delta N_k(u)}{Y(u)}.$$
The convention at $u=0$ allows a baseline event; when there is none, these
formulas agree with the $(0,t]$ product-limit convention in
[[def-nelson-aalen-kaplan-meier-greenwood-estimators]].

This procedure is a finite-sample definition, not a consistency or variance
theorem. A common sampling setup for interpreting it as an estimator of a
population law has IID subject records ([[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]),
independent censoring $C\perp(T,D)$ ([[def-independent-random-elements]]), and
$\mathbb P(C\ge t)>0$, a positive censoring-support condition through $t$.
These are model assumptions, not consequences of the formula.
This item does not invoke a counting-process compensator, martingale bracket,
or process-limit result.

An **event time** is a measurable real-valued map $T$ with values in $[0,\infty)$. A **covariate** is a measurable map $Z$ into a specified standard-Borel space $(\mathcal Z,\mathcal B)$, where standard Borel means measurably isomorphic to a Polish space ([[def-standard-borel-space]]). A **censoring or inspection time** is a measurable real-valued map $C$ with values in $[0,\infty)$. When conditional laws are used, they are probability kernels $K_T(z,\cdot)$ and $K_C(z,\cdot)$ in the sense of [[def-conditional-law-given-a-random-element]] and [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]. They are part of the specified model; their existence for real-valued targets and factorization through standard-Borel $Z$ follow under [[def-axiom-of-choice]] from [[thm-existence-of-regular-conditional-distributions-for-standard-borel-targets]] and [[lem-regular-conditional-kernels-factor-through-a-standard-borel-conditioning-variable]].

The notation $T\perp\!\!\!\perp C\mid\sigma(Z)$ has the meaning in [[def-conditional-independence-given-a-sigma-algebra]]: for bounded measurable $a,b$, $\mathbb E[a(T)b(C)\mid\sigma(Z)]=\mathbb E[a(T)\mid\sigma(Z)]\mathbb E[b(C)\mid\sigma(Z)]$ almost surely. It is a model assumption about the conditional observation law, not a consequence of adjusting for $Z$ and not an empirical conclusion.

Under **right censoring**, the recorded pair is $U=\min(T,C)$ and $\delta=1\{T\le C\}$. Thus $\delta=1$ records an event at $U=T$, including a tie, while $\delta=0$ records censoring at $U=C$ and implies $T>C$. **Left censoring** at a known threshold $L$ records only $T\le L$. **Interval censoring** at known endpoints $L<R$ records $L<T\le R$. **Current-status observation** at an inspection time $C$ records only $\delta_C=1\{T\le C\}$.

**Left truncation**, also called delayed entry at $L$, selects a unit into the sample only when $T>L$; observation begins after that selection. **Right truncation** at $R$ selects a unit only when $T<R$. These are selection rules before the observed sample is formed, whereas censoring coarsens an event time after sampling. The strict and weak inequalities in these definitions fix the endpoint conventions. A random observation endpoint is called noninformative here only when it is fixed by design or is generated independently of $T$ conditional on the stated covariates under a parameter-distinct law; otherwise its joint observation law must be modeled.

For a positive integer sample size $n$, let $(T_i,C_i)$, $1\le i\le n$, be event and censoring times with right-censored observations $(U_i,\delta_i)$ as in [[def-event-time-observation-schemes]], so $U_i=\min(T_i,C_i)$ and $\delta_i=\mathbf 1\{T_i\le C_i\}$. The subject counting process and at-risk process are $N_i(t)=\mathbf 1\{U_i\le t,\ \delta_i=1\}$ and $Y_i(t)=\mathbf 1\{U_i\ge t\}$.
The endpoint convention makes $Y_i$ left-continuous at $U_i$: a subject is still at risk at the observed time, including a tied event and censoring time. Set $N_n=\sum_{i=1}^nN_i$ and $Y_n=\sum_{i=1}^nY_i$. Let $dN_n$ be the finite counting measure of observed events on $[0,\infty)$, with atom $\Delta N_n(u):=\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf 1\{U_i=u,\ \delta_i=1\}$ at each $u\ge0$; in particular, $\Delta N_n(0)=N_n(0)$. Tied failures at $u$ contribute their full count and censorings at $u$ do not contribute to $dN_n(u)$.

For $t\ge0$, the **Nelson–Aalen estimator** is $\widehat\Lambda_n(t)=\int_{[0,t]}\frac{\mathbf 1\{Y_n(u)>0\}}{Y_n(u)}\,dN_n(u)$, where the integrand is defined to be zero when $Y_n(u)=0$. The **Kaplan–Meier estimator** is $\widehat S_n(t)=\prod_{\substack{0\le u\le t:\,\Delta N_n(u)>0}}\left(1-\frac{\Delta N_n(u)}{Y_n(u)}\right)$.
Each product is finite and a factor is zero if every subject at risk fails at that time. The target survival function is $S(t)=P(T>t)$. If $T$ has density $f$, $S$ is positive on the horizon, and $\lambda=f/S$, the continuous cumulative hazard is $\Lambda(t)=\int_0^t\lambda(u)\,du=-\log S(t)$.

These inclusive endpoint formulas reduce to the usual $(0,t]$ formulas whenever $\Delta N_n(0)=0$. If $T$ has finite support $0\le a_1<\cdots<a_m$, write $q_j=P(T=a_j\mid T\ge a_j)$; the corresponding discrete cumulative hazard is $\Lambda_d(t)=\sum_{a_j\le t}q_j$. Under IID sampling, independent censoring, and positive risk probability at the support points, the Nelson–Aalen increments estimate these $q_j$; in general this discrete cumulative hazard is not $-\log S(t)$.

A baseline event is included at $u=0$; if it occurs then $N_i(0)=1$, so a model contract requiring $N_i(0)=0$ must exclude this case.

An empty event product is $1$, and an empty Greenwood event sum is $0$.

On a horizon where every event contribution has $Y_n(u)-\Delta N_n(u)>0$, the **Greenwood variance estimate** is $\widehat V_G(t)=\widehat S_n(t)^2\sum_{0\le u\le t:\,\Delta N_n(u)>0}\frac{\Delta N_n(u)}{Y_n(u)\{Y_n(u)-\Delta N_n(u)\}}$.
Greenwood's formula is used as a first-order asymptotic variance estimate when the sampling and censoring assumptions justify that approximation; the formula alone asserts no asymptotic result and is not an exact finite-sample variance identity. It is undefined when a contributing denominator is zero.

For each fixed $t$, these are statistics of the observed sample in the sense of [[def-statistic-and-estimator]]. To express event-time sums and products as fixed finite operations, scan indices $i=1,\ldots,n$ and include only the first event observation at each distinct time; each inclusion condition uses finitely many Borel equalities and inequalities among the observed $U_i$ and $\delta_i$. Risk and event counts are finite Borel sums, and every division uses the stated positive-count branch. Greenwood is defined only on its positive-denominator domain.

derivations.claim: At time $1$, both groups have $Y(1)=16$ and $\Delta N_1(1)=4$. The low-CV group has $\Delta N(1)=8$, so $\widehat S(1)=1-8/16=1/2$ and $\widehat F_1(1)=4/16=1/4$. The high-CV group has $\Delta N(1)=12$, so $\widehat S(1)=1-12/16=1/4$ and $\widehat F_1(1)=4/16=1/4$.

At time $2$, the low-CV risk count is $8$ and $\Delta N_1(2)=2$, giving increment $(1/2)(2/8)=1/8$ and $\widehat F_1(2)=1/4+1/8=3/8$. The high-CV risk count is $4$ and $\Delta N_1(2)=1$, giving increment $(1/4)(1/4)=1/16$ and $\widehat F_1(2)=1/4+1/16=5/16$. Thus higher cardiovascular mortality lowers the observed cancer cumulative incidence even though both groups have cause-1 event fractions $1/4$ at each event time.

If cause-2 deaths are instead recoded as censorings for the cause-1 Kaplan–Meier calculation, the low-CV product is $(1-4/16)(1-2/8)=(3/4)^2=9/16$, and the high-CV product is $(1-4/16)(1-1/4)=(3/4)^2=9/16$. Both complements are $7/16$, which differs from both observed cause-1 incidences, $3/8$ and $5/16$. The cause-specific product-limit complement therefore does not equal the observed cause-specific cumulative incidence in these records.
